thread.title: NWLC finds waiting lists for child care assistance nearly doubled in 2025
thread.title_full: NWLC finds waiting lists for child care assistance nearly doubled in 2025

author: First State Times
title: NWLC finds waiting lists for child care assistance nearly doubled in 2025
text:
The National Women’s Law Center announced on May 20 that the number of children placed on waiting lists for federally funded child care assistance nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025, with the total continuing to grow. The findings come from the organization’s annual State Child Care Assistance Policies report.
The increase in waiting lists is significant for families seeking support and for early educators, as it highlights ongoing challenges in accessing affordable child care. The report is intended to help state lawmakers, advocates, and policymakers track progress or setbacks in child care policies across the country.
“This deeply troubling increase in the number of children on child care waiting lists is the result of a failure to invest in this crucial sector,” said Karen Schulman, senior director of state child care policy and author of the report. “Since the expiration of tens of billions of dollars in federal child care funding in 2023 and 2024, an already fragile child care system has been pushed even closer to the brink. Yet Congress has not responded, and a series of actions by the Trump administration has only further destabilized a sector that families and the economy depend on. These alarming numbers should be a wake-up call for lawmakers to invest in child care and help families struggling to keep up with relentlessly rising costs.”
According to key findings from the report, seventeen states had either waiting lists or froze intake for child care assistance as of February 2025, compared with thirteen states one year earlier. Approximately 106,700 children were added to waiting lists nationwide between February 2024 and February 2025—an increase that brought total enrollment on such lists up by ninety percent over that period. The trend continued through summer and fall of 2025 when more than an additional 175,000 children were added—a seventy-eight percent jump over just a few months.
At least seven states newly began placing families on waiting lists or freezing intake after February 2025; at least ten other states saw their existing waitlists grow during this time frame. The full report also provides state-by-state data covering income eligibility limits, parent copayments, provider payment rates, and eligibility rules related to parents searching for work.
The National Women’s Law Center encourages readers interested in further details about these trends or specific policy information by state to consult its full report: Warning Signs: State Child Care Assistance Policies 2025.
